source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb; 8.5; 9.4; 9.5; 9.6; 20.5

main.t: The medial bone of the forearm, on the little-finger side (ulna).

simpler.t: The ulna is the forearm bone on the little-finger side.

deeper.t: Its hooked upper end grips the humerus and forms the hinge of the elbow.

facts.t: It runs from the elbow to the wrist, parallel to the radius, on the medial side.
Its upper end forms the bony point of the elbow.
At the wrist it does not touch the carpal bones directly.

simpler.t: It runs from the point of your elbow down to the little-finger side of your wrist.

deeper.t: A pad of fibrocartilage between the radius and the ulna’s styloid process meets the triquetrum.

items.name: Trochlear notch
items.t: A large C-shaped hollow, like a crescent spanner. It wraps around the trochlea of the humerus.

items.name: Olecranon
items.t: The bony point of the elbow. It fits into the olecranon fossa of the humerus when the elbow straightens.

items.name: Coronoid process
items.t: The lip below the notch. It fits into the coronoid fossa when the elbow bends fully.

items.name: Radial notch
items.t: A small smooth area beside the notch, where the head of the radius turns.

items.name: Ulnar tuberosity
items.t: A rough area on the front, just below the coronoid process.

items.name: Interosseous border
items.t: A ridge on the outer side of the shaft. The interosseous membrane attaches along it.

items.name: Head and styloid process
items.t: The small rounded lower end, with a short projection behind it.

simpler.t: Its big hooked top end wraps around the humerus; its small head is at the wrist.

deeper.t: The ulna’s head is at its lower end. The radius is the other way round: its head is at the elbow.

facts.t: The C-shaped notch wraps around the pulley-shaped trochlea, so the elbow can only bend and straighten.
The olecranon and coronoid process fit into hollows of the humerus. So the elbow can straighten and bend fully.
In pronation, it is the radius that turns; its lower end crosses over the ulna.

simpler.t: Its hook makes a strong hinge, so your elbow bends and straightens like a door.

items.name: Elbow (humeroulnar) joint
items.t: A uniaxial hinge joint between the trochlea and the trochlear notch.

items.name: Proximal radioulnar joint
items.t: The radial notch meets the head of the radius.

items.name: Distal radioulnar joint
items.t: Its head meets the ulnar notch of the radius.

items.name: Ulnar collateral ligament
items.t: A triangular band from the medial epicondyle to the inner side of the upper ulna.

items.name: Interosseous membrane
items.t: Joins the shafts of the ulna and radius.

items.name: Ulnar artery
items.t: Runs down the forearm alongside the ulna to the wrist.

items.name: Ulnar nerve
items.t: Passes behind the medial epicondyle and enters the forearm beside the ulna.

simpler.t: It hinges with the humerus and joins the radius at both ends.

facts.t: It forms by replacing a cartilage model with bone (endochondral ossification).
Bone first appears in the shaft by about the twelfth week. Centres in the ends appear later, usually after birth.
With the elbow straight, the forearm angles 5–15 degrees outwards from the arm (the carrying angle).
The carrying angle is larger in females, to clear their wider pelvis.

items.injury: Repeated forceful straightening of the forearm, as in baseball pitching.
items.damaged: The ulnar collateral ligament on the inner side of the elbow.
items.cannotDo: Throw forcefully; the ligament may need reconstruction (“Tommy John surgery”).
items.why: This ligament stops the elbow moving sideways and over-straightening; its front part resists over-straightening most.

items.injury: A fall onto the point of the elbow.
items.why: The muscle that straightens the elbow (triceps) pulls on the olecranon, drawing the fragment away.

items.q: Explain why the elbow can only bend and straighten.
model: The humeroulnar joint is a hinge joint.
The C-shaped trochlear notch wraps around the pulley-shaped trochlea.
This allows movement around a single axis.
Strong collateral ligaments also prevent side-to-side movement.

items.q: Compare the upper and lower ends of the ulna and the radius.
model: Ulna: a large upper end with the trochlear notch, and a small head below.
Radius: a small disc-shaped head above, and a broad lower end.
The lower end of the radius meets two carpal bones.
The lower end of the ulna does not touch the carpal bones directly.

items.q: A baseball pitcher has pain on the inner side of the elbow when throwing. Predict the injured structure and its normal job.
model: It runs from the medial epicondyle to the inner side of the upper ulna.
It stops sideways movement and over-straightening of the elbow.
Forceful repeated throwing strains it; it may need reconstruction.

check.stem: Which part of the ulna forms the bony point of the elbow?
check.why: The olecranon forms the bony tip of the elbow.

check.stem: Which bone does the trochlear notch of the ulna meet?
check.why: It wraps around the trochlea of the humerus at the elbow.

options: The angle of the radial head
The bend of the wrist in a Colles fracture
The angle between the hand and the forearm
The outward angle of the forearm from the arm
check.why: With the elbow straight, the forearm angles 5–15 degrees outwards from the arm.
